stories.summary: Growing up in protectionist India, Ajay couldn't buy modern electronics legally — they were either unavailable or smuggled. His most prized purchase of those years was an early chess computer with a tiny LED that would blink to suggest moves; a neighbour flying to Singapore had to bring it back for him. It was an exotic, almost magical object — and it was contraband by another name.
stories.insight: Protectionism doesn't actually keep technology out — it just routes it through black markets, makes it more expensive, and humiliates citizens by forcing them to ask for favours from anyone who can travel. The 'self-reliance' justification hides the reality that you've simply made a small, lucky elite the only people with access.

stories.topic: Black Markets For Microchips In Shanghai And Kazakhstan
stories.summary: In 2024, the same subterranean economy Ajay grew up under has reappeared — but now on the other side. Walk into Shanghai and you 'go nudge nudge, hint hint, wink wink' to find the right dealer for an Nvidia A100 chip. In Kazakhstan, people fly in from New Delhi with suitcases of chips to sell at a profit in Central Asia.
stories.insight: History doesn't repeat, but it rhymes brutally. The very architecture of evasion — the trusted middleman, the suitcase, the wink — is the same whether the closed economy is India in 1980 or China in 2024. Closing borders to high-tech merely moves the trade underground; it never stops it.

stories.topic: Seven-Year Waiting List For A New Car
stories.summary: To convey to viewers born after 1991 just how absurd Indian protectionism was, Ajay offers a single image: a secondhand car cost more than a new car. Why? Because a new car had a seven-year waiting list. A used car — whatever its condition — was available immediately, and so commanded the premium.
stories.insight: When the price of a used good exceeds the new good, you are not in a market — you are in a queue. Every shortage economy ends up there, and the inversion of normal price signals is the surest sign that the planning system has broken.

stories.topic: Building NSE's Risk System On Cheap Intel Boxes
stories.summary: In the early 90s, NSE wanted real-time, participant-level derivatives risk management — a level of sophistication beyond anything in the world. Ashish Chauhan and Susan Thomas were sent to Chicago to choose between the CME and CBOT systems; both turned out to be 70s-era and inadequate. Susan proposed a Beowulf cluster — many cheap Intel CPUs strung together in parallel. NSE leadership thought this was crazy; Ravi Narayan split the difference by funding a proof-of-concept at IGIDR with Shovam Mishra. The proof-of-concept hit 100 trades and 200 calculations per second — beyond what the Chicago systems could do — and became 'PR,' the risk system that still runs NSE derivatives trading today.
stories.insight: Embarrassingly parallel computation is the great equalizer: if a problem can be split across CPUs, then 1,000 weak chips beat 10 powerful ones. This is the deepest reason export controls on bleeding-edge GPUs may not work as advertised — a determined engineer can usually substitute many for one.

stories.summary: Throughout the 20th century, Ajay says, there has been a 'sense in America that China is our responsibility' — that helping China progress was a moral mission, not just a transactional foreign policy. After Nixon re-established economic relations in 1972 and Deng came to power in 1978, American society and state signed onto the China project with genuine enthusiasm. Ajay says he has seen this idealism face-to-face in conversations and that Indians find it hard to even visualize.
stories.insight: The unwinding of US–China engagement isn't just realpolitik — it's the death of an idealistic, almost missionary American belief. Understanding the psychology of the prior consensus matters because policy reversals from idealism always carry more emotional charge than reversals from cynicism.

stories.summary: Riffing off Noah Smith, Amit raises the case of DJI and Chinese drone dominance. America's response is to impose export restrictions. But there is a second response: deregulate the domestic drone industry so Americans can build their own. Amit's preferred analogy: if local doctors aren't good enough, you don't 'cure' the patient by banning foreign doctors — you whip your local doctors into shape by exposing them to competition.
stories.insight: The cleanest test of whether a country actually wants to compete: does it remove its own constraints first, or does it reach for the foreigner's leash? Most 'industrial strategy' is the second; the first is harder, slower, and generally what works.

recommendations.item: When the Chips Are Down
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
recommendations.context: An accessible book on the geopolitics and economics of the semiconductor industry by Pranay Kotasthane (a friend of both hosts) and Abhiram Manchi.
recommendations.reason: Demystifies the semiconductor wars and what's really going on in the chip industry — pairs naturally with Chris Miller's Chip War for understanding the stakes of the current US-China tech competition.

recommendations.item: Chip War
recommendations.creator: Chris Miller
recommendations.context: A comprehensive history of the semiconductor industry and the global competition over chip manufacturing.
recommendations.reason: The definitive book for understanding the origins and current stakes of the global tech competition — the intricate supply chains, the strategic importance of chips, and the historical arc that led to today's export controls.

recommendations.item: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
recommendations.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
recommendations.context: Yuen Yuen Ang's analysis of China's economic development model.
recommendations.reason: Critical for understanding what actually happened in China over the last thirty years — Amit cites this to explain why he doesn't buy a 'caricaturish' good-vs-evil Cold War view of China, even as he agrees with criticisms of Xi Jinping.

recommendations.item: China's Gilded Age
recommendations.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
recommendations.context: Yuen Yuen Ang's companion book on corruption and political economy in China's growth story.
recommendations.reason: The darker complement to How China Escaped the Poverty Trap — examines the role of corruption and the evolving political economy that shaped the Chinese miracle, completing a more honest picture of what happened.

recommendations.item: Michael Pettis interviewed by Forward Guidance
recommendations.creator: Forward Guidance with Michael Pettis
recommendations.context: A long interview with Michael Pettis, who lives in China, on Chinese macroeconomics, the collapse of the China model, and short-term overproduction.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls Pettis 'one of the world's good experts on China' — the conversation is 'absolutely eye-opening' on the local context of Chinese macroeconomics and the global protectionist response China is now triggering.

recommendations.item: The U.S. Finally Has a Strategy to Compete With China. Will It Work?
recommendations.creator: Greg Ip
recommendations.context: Greg Ip's Wall Street Journal piece detailing the new American bipartisan consensus on China and the structure of the tech war.
recommendations.reason: Amit uses this as the spine of his summary of the 'three-legged stool' (industrial policy, tariffs, export controls) — Ip captures how, in just eight years, US consensus flipped from engagement to confrontation.

recommendations.item: An Act of War: Inside America's Silicon Blockade Against China
recommendations.creator: Alex W. Palmer
recommendations.context: Alex Palmer's New York Times Magazine piece on the FDPR (Foreign Direct Product Rule) and the silicon blockade.
recommendations.reason: The clearest exposition of how extreme US export controls have become — Amit reads from it to show that even items 'made and shipped outside the United States' with no US components can be classified as American and blocked.

recommendations.item: Three holes in the U.S.' economic strategy against China
recommendations.creator: Noah Smith
recommendations.context: Noah Smith's substack post on the gaps in America's economic strategy against China, including drone dominance.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's argument that you can't beat Chinese drone dominance by banning foreign drones — you have to deregulate your domestic industry. A sober counter to triumphalist American 'we have a plan' rhetoric.

recommendations.item: The tech wars are about to enter a fiery new phase
recommendations.creator: The Economist
recommendations.context: An Economist piece on the next escalation of the US-China tech conflict.
recommendations.reason: Amit links this to support his argument that tech and trade wars are bad for the US, bad for China, and bad for the rest of the world — a corrective to the assumption that the architects of these controls are acting in their own interest.

recommendations.item: Knowledge Lost and Knowledge Regained (Episode 63 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE episode, on how civilizations lose and regain knowledge — including the 'I, Pencil' point that no one person knows how to make a pencil.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes it directly: once a country is cut off from international trade, knowledge, and expertise, its ability to participate is fundamentally contaminated. The USSR experience showed that 'self-reliance' under sanctions does not catch up — it falls further behind.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A deep-dive episode on India's 1991 economic reforms.
recommendations.reason: Recommended for any viewer born after 1991 who can't quite imagine what the protectionist era looked like — the secondhand car costing more than a new car is one of many bizarre details from that period.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the foundational case for freedom.
recommendations.reason: Linked alongside the argument that authoritarian systems crush their best minds — the genius 0.01% who would otherwise drive scientific catch-up are the very people destroyed by limits on freedom of speech and dissent.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on India's economic reformers.
recommendations.reason: Linked as part of the 1991 reforms cluster — useful context for the era of Indian protectionism the hosts keep returning to.

recommendations.item: The Three Globalizations (Episode 17 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The EIE episode where Ajay laid out his framework of three successive globalizations.
recommendations.reason: Today's tech war is an intensification of the third globalization story Ajay developed there — access to the core advanced economies is now conditional on military and foreign-policy good behaviour, not unconditional.

recommendations.item: Dawn of the third globalisation?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's column in which he formulated the third-globalization argument.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommended as the print formulation of the framework that anchors this episode — globalisation has not ended, but it has acquired conditions, and rogue actors are being excluded from the core.

recommendations.item: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode where Ajay argued the Chinese economic model was failing.
recommendations.reason: Background for the 'collapse' point in this episode — Xi Jinping's centralization, the disenchantment of the private sector, the FDI flight, and the macroeconomic meltdown that followed. Ajay says they 'were on the right track' there.

recommendations.item: The case for trade barriers against Chinese imports
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's coauthored piece making a new-trade-theory case for restrictions on Chinese goods — distinct from the military/tech-wars argument.
recommendations.reason: Amit references this to disagree with Ajay — not on the technicalities of new trade theory, but on the broader stance that 'economic warfare is economic warfare.' The piece is the printed form of one half of the disagreement at the heart of this episode.

recommendations.item: The Bureau of Industry and Security sanctions list
recommendations.creator: U.S. Department of Commerce
recommendations.context: The publicly available list of entities sanctioned by the BIS — including roughly 12 Indian companies at the time of recording.
recommendations.reason: Direct, actionable knowledge for anyone in business: hang out on the BIS website, check who's on the sanctioned list, and organise your dealings to avoid them. Being sanctioned cuts you off from US travel, US finance, and US trade — 'you don't want to go there.'

recommendations.item: The Outlaws (Episode 61 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on outlaws, mavericks, and creative dissent.
recommendations.reason: Ajay references it to make the point that the geniuses crushed by authoritarian regimes are precisely the 'mavericks, the crazy people' — the tiny 0.01% who drive breakthroughs. Authoritarianism is bad not just morally but technologically.

recommendations.item: The Semiconductor Wars (Episode 358 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
recommendations.context: Amit's long-form Seen and the Unseen episode on the semiconductor wars with the authors of When the Chips Are Down.
recommendations.reason: The deep-dive companion to Amit's book recommendations — for listeners who want hours of context on the chip industry rather than just the bullet points.

core_ideas.concept: The Three-Legged Stool of Tech War
core_ideas.explanation: America's strategy against China rests on three pillars. First, industrial policy — heavy subsidies to bring strategic manufacturing home (TSMC's three Arizona fabs are the canonical example). Second, tariffs — escalating steadily under both Trump and Biden. Third, export controls — designed to deny China the IP, software, machines, and chips needed to develop indigenous capability. Industrial policy is the carrot for the home team; tariffs and export controls are the sticks for China.
core_ideas.quote: It is industrial policy, tariffs, and export controls.

core_ideas.explanation: A piece of US legislation that effectively makes American export law extraterritorial. Foreign-made items are subject to American controls if they were produced using American technology or software — even if the item is made and shipped outside the US, never crosses US borders, and contains no US-origin components in the final product. This is how the United States reaches into a Dutch fab making chips for a Chinese customer using American software, and stops the deal. Originally aimed at Huawei; now wielded much more broadly.
core_ideas.quote: It is a sweeping assertion of extraterritorial power.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Globalizations and the Conditional Core
core_ideas.explanation: The first and second globalizations made access to the advanced-economy core (~65% of world GDP) effectively unconditional — any periphery country wanting capital, technology, or trade with the core could have it; the only barriers were the periphery's own (e.g. India's tariffs on imports). The third globalization changes the rules: the core now conditions access on good behaviour in military and foreign affairs. China and Russia, by violating those norms, are being progressively excluded. Whether this is wise is debatable; that it has happened is fact.
core_ideas.quote: Access to globalization is no longer a free lunch.

core_ideas.explanation: Through the 20th century, America carried an idealistic, almost missionary belief that it had a civilizing role to play in China. After 1972 and especially after 1989's 'end of history,' the West offered China full participation in globalization — WTO entry under Bill Clinton, with Chinese promises to follow the rules. China largely cheated on those promises. Over time, IP theft, cyber attacks, and rule-breaking accumulated; meanwhile China grew large enough that its misbehaviour materially moved global markets (unlike India's small-country misbehaviour). The Russian invasion of Ukraine, partly funded by European gas and equipped with Western precision tools, made the contradiction unbearable. Finally, Xi Jinping's open posture as a revisionist power on Taiwan and his lethal aid to Russia destroyed the last reservoirs of Western patience. The pivot followed.
core_ideas.quote: Why are we putting lives at stake in Ukraine to overcome a problem that has been enabled by us?

core_ideas.explanation: Many heavy compute problems — derivatives risk, simulation, training large models — are 'embarrassingly parallel': they can be split into independent pieces that don't depend on each other. For such problems, 1,000 cheap CPUs can substitute for 10 elite GPUs. This is what Susan Thomas built at NSE in the early 90s with a Beowulf cluster on Intel boxes, beating Chicago's expensive 70s-era systems. It is also why determined Chinese, Russian, and Indian labs can mostly route around export controls. The blockade buys you delay and inconvenience, not impossibility.
core_ideas.quote: Instead of 10 super-powerful Nvidia GPUs, you'll have 1,000 weaker GPUs and you will get to the same compute.

core_ideas.concept: Sanctions Work Against Races, Not Targets
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framework for predicting sanction effectiveness. Against a fixed objective like 'build a nuclear bomb,' export controls are essentially useless — a determined country will get there eventually with parallelism, ingenuity, and time. But against a race — drones in Ukraine, smartphones in global markets, military gear on a battlefield — being one or two months behind is decisive. In an arms race, the absolute level doesn't matter; the relative gap does. Make the Chinese DJI engineer string together 1,000 cheap CPUs while the NATO equivalent uses Nvidia, and the Ukrainian drone wins on the battlefield this month. That is how sanctions theoretically pay off.
core_ideas.quote: You don't need to indefinitely be better. You only need to be a little bit better.

core_ideas.concept: The Twin Coincidence — Tech War Plus China's Macro Meltdown
core_ideas.explanation: Three distinct stories are running simultaneously and shouldn't be conflated: (a) the third globalization, an analytical fact about how the rules of access have changed; (b) the tech war proper, a military-driven dispute escalating since October 2022; and (c) a uniquely Chinese macroeconomic crisis since 2022-2023, around overproduction, demographic decline, and FDI flight. Conflating them produces sloppy thinking. The episode is about (b), but the timing of (b) coinciding with (c) compounds China's pain and constrains its responses.

core_ideas.concept: Authoritarian Systems Are Bad At Catch-Up
core_ideas.explanation: Self-reliance under sanctions is supposed to galvanize a country: fire in the belly, indigenous innovation. The historical record says otherwise. The USSR was cut off from cutting-edge Western technology, tried hard, and failed — they never built Unix, never built competitive computers. The reason isn't lack of effort; it's the political system. The genius 0.01% who actually drive scientific breakthroughs are the mavericks, dissidents, and outlaws — exactly the people that authoritarian regimes destroy. Limits on freedom of speech and dissent damage the brightest most.
core_ideas.quote: The bests don't flourish when they are crushed under conditions of unfreedom.

core_ideas.concept: The Argument Against Economic Warfare (Amit's Position)
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's principled disagreement with Ajay: free trade is a positive-sum game whose benefits flow to the people on both sides, not the states. Economic warfare hurts citizens, not regimes. The arrogance of the US declaring what counts as the 'global order' and punishing transgressors is not a defensible foundation. Even unilaterally opening trade — letting in cheap Chinese drones, cheap Chinese chips — benefits both populations. 'Crony capitalism is not capitalism' and 'third globalization is not globalization' if it is conditional and selective. The right response to Chinese drone dominance is to deregulate your own industry, not to ban theirs.
core_ideas.quote: Economic warfare is economic warfare, and I'm fundamentally against economic warfare at all times.

core_ideas.concept: The Argument For Selective Economic Pressure (Ajay's Position)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's pragmatic case: in a world where Russia has invaded Ukraine, where Xi Jinping refuses to renounce Taiwan, and where Western technology directly enables enemy munitions, principled free-tradism becomes complicit. If the choice is killing people or interfering with prosperity, choose the latter. Economic warfare is preferable to actual war. This isn't a permanent stance — Ajay still wants conditions of world peace and full globalization — but a response to the specific, present-tense reality of revisionist powers refusing to play by any rules.
core_ideas.quote: If the choice is killing people or interfering with economic prosperity, I would take interfering with economic prosperity.

core_ideas.explanation: The hosts disagree productively. Ajay says Deng failed because his project of turning China into a 'normal country' fell apart — Xi rolled it all back. Amit says Deng was one of the great men of history because he lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and increased the probability of liberal-democratic outcomes; what happened decades later in a deeply complex world isn't his failure. Amit's analogy: would we say Nehru failed because Indira Gandhi later imposed the Emergency? The disagreement is really about how to evaluate statesmen — by intentions and probabilities, or by long-run outcomes.

Ajay quotes Mike Tyson: everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth. The American tech-war plan — the three-legged stool, the FDPR, the BIS sanctions — sounds clean on a whiteboard. But unintended consequences will compound. China is ramping up legacy-chip production and could plausibly wipe out TSMC, Intel, and Samsung's legacy-chip businesses. India's chip ambitions then become harder, not easier. The squeeze on China makes Taiwan more, not less, dangerous. Reflexivity matters. The arrogance — 'we shall shape the world to our will' — is the same arrogance that built the mujahideen against the Soviets and got 9/11 in return.
core_ideas.quote: Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens with: 'I have the white hair to prove it' — establishing his credibility on the deep past of Indian protectionism.
Amit, on the BIS sanctions regime: 'At the risk of being sanctioned by the US BIS, I will say that the US BIS should be renamed USBS.'
Amit on the American tech-war strategy: 'all of this rationale sounds great and as Donald Trump would say in all caps WE HAVE THE BEST PLANS.'
Ajay's reply via Mike Tyson: 'Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.' Amit's pedantic correction: 'It's not everybody, it's everyone.'

Amit's free-trade analogy: if local doctors aren't good enough, you don't ban foreign doctors — 'because then the patient will die.' You whip your local doctors into shape by exposing them to competition.

Francis Fukuyama's 'end of history' — invoked twice as the worldview that produced the 1990s engagement consensus, and as the worldview now being decisively buried by US-China decoupling. Amit notes the phrase is 'often misinterpreted.'
The 'Golden Arches' theory of peace — the old saying that two countries with McDonald's have never gone to war. Ajay's update: 'Russia invaded Ukraine and both countries had McDonald's.'
Persia vs Athens — Ajay's framing of the post-1989 mood: 'this entire nightmare of 2,000 years of fighting between Persia and Athens has come to an end, and Athens won.'

Beowulf cluster — the technique of stringing together cheap commodity CPUs for parallel computing, named after the Old English epic. Used by Susan Thomas at NSE in the early 90s and now the metaphor for how sanctioned states route around chip blockades.

The mujahideen / Osama bin Laden parable — Amit invokes America's funding of Afghan guerrillas against the Soviets as the canonical lesson on the unintended consequences of trying to 'shape the world to our will.'

'Revisionist power' — the foreign-policy term for a country that fundamentally questions the international order and seeks to disrupt it by force. Ajay applies it to Xi Jinping's China after his Taiwan rhetoric and lethal aid to Russia.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) — Ajay's spotlight on 'an obscure United States federal agency' that may be the most consequential government body you've never heard of. At its Cold War peak it issued 100,000 export licenses a year; that fell to 10,000 in the 1990s and is now back to 40,000.
